notes.definition: The Haber process manufactures ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen in a reversible reaction, N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, using an iron catalyst at about 450 °C and about 200 atmospheres. Ammonia is used to make nitrogen-based fertilisers.
explanation: The Haber process is used to manufacture ammonia, which can be used to produce nitrogen-based fertilisers. The raw materials are nitrogen and hydrogen. Nitrogen is obtained from the air (which is about 78% nitrogen). Hydrogen may be obtained from natural gas (methane) or other sources. The reaction is: nitrogen + hydrogen ⇌ ammonia, or N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g). The forward reaction is exothermic.

The purified gases are passed over a catalyst of iron at a high temperature (about 450 °C) and a high pressure (about 200 atmospheres). Some of the hydrogen and nitrogen reacts to form ammonia. The reaction is reversible, so some of the ammonia produced breaks down into nitrogen and hydrogen. Only a fraction of the gases is converted on each pass through the reactor.

The gas mixture leaving the reactor is cooled. On cooling, the ammonia liquefies (it has a much higher boiling point than nitrogen and hydrogen) and is removed. The remaining hydrogen and nitrogen are recycled back into the reactor. Recycling means that, over time, almost all of the nitrogen and hydrogen is converted into ammonia, so very little raw material is wasted.

Higher tier: the conditions are chosen using ideas about equilibrium and rate. The forward reaction reduces the number of molecules of gas (4 molecules on the left, 2 on the right), so increasing the pressure shifts the position of equilibrium to the right, increasing the yield of ammonia; higher pressure also increases the rate. But very high pressures need expensive, thick-walled equipment and a lot of energy for compressing the gases, and are more dangerous. About 200 atmospheres is a compromise between yield and cost and safety.

Higher tier: because the forward reaction is exothermic, a lower temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right and gives a higher yield, but the rate of reaction would be too slow. A higher temperature gives a faster rate but a lower equilibrium yield. About 450 °C is a compromise temperature that gives a reasonable yield at an acceptable rate. The iron catalyst increases the rate of both forward and reverse reactions equally, so it does not change the position of equilibrium or the yield, but it means equilibrium is reached faster, so a lower temperature can be used than without a catalyst, saving energy. The commercially used conditions balance the availability and cost of raw materials and energy, the control of the equilibrium position and the rate.
keyFacts: Haber process: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (reversible; forward reaction exothermic).
Ammonia is used to make nitrogen-based fertilisers.
Nitrogen comes from the air; hydrogen from natural gas or other sources.
Conditions: iron catalyst, about 450 °C, about 200 atmospheres.
Ammonia is removed by cooling, which liquefies it.
Unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled.
Higher: high pressure favours ammonia (fewer gas molecules on the right) but is expensive and dangerous.
Higher: low temperature favours ammonia (exothermic) but is too slow; 450 °C is a compromise.
Higher: the catalyst speeds up the rate but does not change the yield.

keyTerms.definition: The industrial process that makes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen using an iron catalyst.
A reaction in which the products can react to re-form the reactants, shown by ⇌.
In a closed system, the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate, so the amounts of reactants and products stay constant.
The amount (or percentage) of ammonia in the equilibrium mixture, or the amount of product obtained.
Conditions that balance a reasonable yield against an acceptable rate and cost.
A substance that increases the rate of a reaction without being used up; iron in the Haber process.
Returning unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen to the reactor so they are not wasted.

equations.name: Percentage yield
equations.formula: percentage yield = (mass of product actually made ÷ maximum theoretical mass of product) × 100

workedExamples.title: Theoretical mass and percentage yield
workedExamples.question: A reactor converts 56 tonnes of nitrogen. Calculate the maximum mass of ammonia that could form. If 51 tonnes of ammonia are actually produced, calculate the percentage yield. (Mr: N₂ = 28, NH₃ = 17)
steps: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃: 1 mol N₂ gives 2 mol NH₃, so 28 g of N₂ gives 2 × 17 = 34 g of NH₃.
56 tonnes of N₂ is 2 × 28, so maximum NH₃ = 2 × 34 = 68 tonnes.

workedExamples.title: Reading yield data (graph)
workedExamples.question: Equilibrium yields of ammonia: at 450 °C, 100 atm 16%, 200 atm 28%, 300 atm 36%. At 350 °C, 200 atm 52%. Describe the effect of pressure at 450 °C and of temperature at 200 atm.
steps: At 450 °C, as pressure increases from 100 to 300 atm the yield increases from 16% to 36%.
At 200 atm, lowering the temperature from 450 °C to 350 °C increases the yield from 28% to 52%.
Increase in yield at 200 atm = 52 − 28 = 24 percentage points.
workedExamples.answer: Higher pressure and lower temperature both increase the equilibrium yield.

workedExamples.title: Volumes of gases
workedExamples.question: What volume of hydrogen reacts with 150 dm³ of nitrogen, and what volume of ammonia forms if all reacts? (All volumes at the same temperature and pressure.)
steps: Ratio of volumes N₂ : H₂ : NH₃ = 1 : 3 : 2 (equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the catalyst increases the yield of ammonia.
misconceptions.right: In fact the iron catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but the yield is unchanged.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think 450 °C is used because it gives the highest yield.
misconceptions.right: In fact a lower temperature gives a higher yield; 450 °C is a compromise that gives a reasonable yield at an acceptable rate.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all the nitrogen and hydrogen is converted on one pass.
misconceptions.right: In fact only a fraction reacts each pass; the unreacted gases are recycled, so eventually most is converted.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think ammonia is removed as a gas.
misconceptions.right: In fact the mixture is cooled so ammonia liquefies and is removed as a liquid, while nitrogen and hydrogen stay as gases.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think pressure is kept at 200 atm because higher pressure lowers the yield.
misconceptions.right: In fact higher pressure would increase the yield, but the equipment and energy costs and safety risks would be too great.

realWorld: About 80% of the ammonia produced worldwide is used to make fertilisers such as ammonium nitrate.
Ammonia plants are often built next to natural gas supplies because methane is the main source of hydrogen.
The Haber process made it possible to grow enough food for billions more people, but uses about 1 to 2% of the world's energy.
higherTier: Interpret graphs of reaction conditions versus rate and yield.

Pressure: the forward reaction produces fewer molecules of gas (4 → 2), so higher pressure shifts equilibrium to the right, increasing yield (and rate); limited by the cost of equipment, energy for compression and safety.
Temperature: the forward reaction is exothermic, so lower temperature increases yield but decreases rate; about 450 °C is a compromise between rate and yield.
The iron catalyst increases rate but does not affect the position of equilibrium.
Commercial conditions balance the availability and cost of raw materials and energy, control of the equilibrium position and rate.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is for separate Chemistry (8462) only.
The Haber process: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, iron catalyst, about 450 °C, about 200 atmospheres; ammonia liquefied and removed; unreacted gases recycled.
Nitrogen from the air; hydrogen from natural gas or other sources; ammonia used to make nitrogen-based fertilisers.
examTips: Learn the conditions as a set: iron catalyst, about 450 °C, about 200 atmospheres.
State where the raw materials come from: nitrogen from air, hydrogen from natural gas.
Higher: for each condition give both sides: effect on yield AND effect on rate or cost, then say it is a compromise.
Higher: always count gas molecules (4 on the left, 2 on the right) when explaining the effect of pressure.
Never say the catalyst increases yield; it only increases rate.
When reading a yield graph, read values carefully and quote them with units (% and atm or °C).
summary: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃; ammonia is used for fertilisers.
N₂ from air; H₂ from natural gas.
Ammonia liquefied by cooling and removed; unreacted gases recycled.
Higher: high pressure increases yield but costs more; 450 °C is a rate/yield compromise.
Higher: catalyst speeds up the reaction without changing the yield.

options: By cooling, so the ammonia liquefies
By dissolving the nitrogen in water
markScheme: 1 mark: cooling so ammonia liquefies
questions.explanation: Ammonia has a much higher boiling point than nitrogen and hydrogen, so it condenses first on cooling.

questions.question: Which is the balanced equation for the Haber process?
markScheme: 1 mark: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃
questions.explanation: Nitrogen and hydrogen are diatomic. Two N and six H on each side.

questions.question: Why are the unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen recycled?
options: So they are not wasted and more ammonia can be made from them
markScheme: 1 mark: so they are not wasted / can be converted into ammonia
questions.explanation: Only a fraction reacts on each pass, so recycling means nearly all the raw materials are eventually converted.

questions.question: What is the effect of the iron catalyst on the Haber process?
options: It shifts the equilibrium to the right
It increases the yield of ammonia
It increases the rate at which equilibrium is reached without changing the yield
markScheme: 1 mark: increases rate, no change in yield
questions.explanation: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so the equilibrium position is unchanged.

questions.question: Why does increasing the pressure increase the equilibrium yield of ammonia?
options: There are fewer molecules of gas on the right-hand side of the equation
The catalyst works better at high pressure
Ammonia is a liquid at high pressure
markScheme: 1 mark: fewer molecules of gas on the right
questions.explanation: 4 molecules of gas form 2 molecules, so increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium towards ammonia to reduce the pressure.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows how the equilibrium yield of ammonia in the Haber process changes with pressure at three different temperatures.
The forward reaction in the Haber process is exothermic.
What happens to the equilibrium yield of ammonia if the temperature is increased?
options: It increases and then becomes zero
markScheme: 1 mark: it decreases
questions.explanation: Increasing temperature favours the endothermic (reverse) reaction, so less ammonia is present at equilibrium, although the rate increases.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows how the equilibrium yield of ammonia in the Haber process changes with pressure at three different temperatures.
Determine the difference in the equilibrium yield of ammonia between 350 °C and 450 °C at 200 atmospheres.
markScheme: 1 mark: 52 − 28 = 24 (percentage points)
questions.explanation: From Figure 1 at 200 atmospheres: 52% at 350 °C and 28% at 450 °C. 52 − 28 = 24. The lower temperature gives a yield 24 percentage points higher.

questions.question:
The equation for the Haber process is:
N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃
Calculate the maximum mass of ammonia that can be made from 14 tonnes of nitrogen.
Relative formula masses (Mr): N₂ = 28   NH₃ = 17
markScheme: 1 mark: 28 tonnes of N₂ gives 2 × 17 = 34 tonnes of NH₃
1 mark: 14 tonnes gives 17 tonnes
questions.explanation: 28 → 2 × 17 = 34. 14 is half of 28, so half of 34 = 17 tonnes.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows information about one pass of the reactants through the reactor in a Haber process plant.
Calculate the percentage yield for a single pass.

headers: Maximum mass of ammonia that could be made in tonnes
Mass of ammonia actually made in tonnes

markScheme: 1 mark: 30%
questions.explanation: Percentage yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100 = 30%.

questions.question:
The equation for the Haber process is:
N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃
Calculate the mass of hydrogen needed to react completely with 840 kg of nitrogen.
Relative formula masses (Mr): N₂ = 28   H₂ = 2
markScheme: 1 mark: moles N₂ = 840 000 ÷ 28 = 30 000 mol (or 840 ÷ 28 = 30 kmol)
1 mark: moles H₂ = 3 × 30 000 = 90 000 mol
questions.explanation: 1 mol N₂ reacts with 3 mol H₂, so 28 g of N₂ reacts with 6 g of H₂. 840 × 6 ÷ 28 = 180 kg.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows how the equilibrium yield of ammonia in the Haber process changes with pressure at three different temperatures.
Calculate the percentage increase in the equilibrium yield of ammonia at 450 °C when the pressure is increased from 200 atmospheres to 400 atmospheres.
Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
markScheme: 1 mark: 50%
questions.explanation: From Figure 1 at 450 °C: 28% at 200 atmospheres and 42% at 400 atmospheres. The yield rises by 14 percentage points, which is a 50% increase on 28%. Doubling the pressure does not double the yield, which helps explain why 200 atmospheres is chosen.

questions.question:
60 dm³ of nitrogen reacts completely with hydrogen.
N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g)
All volumes are measured at the same temperature and pressure.
Calculate the volume of ammonia formed.
markScheme: 1 mark: volume ratio N₂ : NH₃ = 1 : 2
1 mark: ammonia = 2 × 60 = 120 dm³
questions.explanation: Equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules, so volumes are in the same ratio as moles: N₂ : H₂ : NH₃ = 1 : 3 : 2. (The hydrogen needed would be 180 dm³.)

questions.question: Name the two raw materials for the Haber process and give a source of each.
markScheme: 1 mark: nitrogen from the air
1 mark: hydrogen from natural gas (methane) or other sources
questions.explanation: Both gases are purified before entering the reactor.

questions.question: State one major use of the ammonia made in the Haber process.
markScheme: 1 mark: making (nitrogen-based) fertilisers
questions.explanation: Most ammonia is used for fertilisers such as ammonium nitrate.

questions.question: State what the symbol ⇌ tells you about the Haber process reaction.
markScheme: 1 mark: the reaction is reversible
questions.explanation: Some ammonia breaks down into nitrogen and hydrogen.

questions.question: Describe what happens to the gas mixture after it leaves the reactor.
markScheme: 1 mark: it is cooled so the ammonia liquefies and is removed
1 mark: the unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled to the reactor
questions.explanation: Recycling makes the overall process efficient.

questions.question: Explain why a pressure higher than 200 atmospheres is not used, even though it would increase the yield.
markScheme: 1 mark: very high pressures need expensive, strong equipment / more energy to compress gases
1 mark: risk of explosion / dangerous, so the extra yield is not worth the cost
questions.explanation: 200 atm is a compromise between yield and cost and safety.

questions.question: Explain why a temperature of about 450 °C is used in the Haber process.
markScheme: 1 mark: the forward reaction is exothermic, so a lower temperature would give a higher yield
1 mark: but at a lower temperature the rate would be too slow
1 mark: 450 °C is a compromise giving a reasonable yield at an acceptable rate
questions.explanation: Rate and yield pull in opposite directions for temperature.

questions.question: Suggest how using an iron catalyst helps reduce the energy costs of the Haber process.
markScheme: 1 mark: the catalyst increases the rate (equilibrium reached faster)
1 mark: so an acceptable rate is achieved at a lower temperature, needing less energy for heating
questions.explanation: Without a catalyst, a much higher temperature would be needed for a useful rate, lowering yield and costing more.

questions.question: Only about 15% of the nitrogen and hydrogen is converted into ammonia each time the gases pass through the reactor. Explain why the process still converts most of the raw materials into ammonia.
markScheme: 1 mark: unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled
1 mark: so they pass through the reactor again and again until most is converted
questions.explanation: Recycling means the low conversion per pass is not wasteful.

questions.question: Describe how ammonia is manufactured in the Haber process. Include the raw materials, the conditions and what happens to the products.
markScheme: Indicative content: nitrogen from air, hydrogen from natural gas; gases purified; passed over iron catalyst; about 450 °C; about 200 atmospheres; N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃; reversible, so only some converts; gases cooled; ammonia liquefies and is removed; unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen recycled.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): raw materials and all three conditions given, with separation by cooling and recycling described.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some conditions or raw materials stated.
questions.explanation: Cover sources, conditions, separation and recycling in a logical order.

questions.question:
The equation for the Haber process is:
N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)
The forward reaction is exothermic.
The conditions used are an iron catalyst, a temperature of about 450 °C and a pressure of about 200 atmospheres.
Explain, using ideas about equilibrium and rate, why these conditions are chosen as a compromise.
markScheme: Indicative content: Pressure: 4 molecules of gas on left, 2 on right; increasing pressure shifts equilibrium right, increasing yield; higher pressure also increases rate (particles closer, more frequent collisions); but higher pressures need stronger, more expensive equipment, more energy for compression and are more dangerous; 200 atm is a compromise. Temperature: forward reaction exothermic, so lower temperature shifts equilibrium right and increases yield; but lower temperature reduces rate (fewer successful collisions); 450 °C is a compromise between yield and rate. Catalyst: iron increases rate by providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy; does not change yield or equilibrium position; allows lower temperature, saving energy. Unreacted gases recycled so low yield per pass is acceptable.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): explains the effects of both temperature and pressure on yield and rate, with the reasons for compromise, and correctly describes the role of the catalyst.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains the effect of temperature or pressure on yield with some reference to rate or cost.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example 'high pressure gives more ammonia'.
questions.explanation: Strong answers explain both sides of the compromise for each condition, rather than just stating the conditions.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows how the equilibrium yield of ammonia in the Haber process changes with pressure at three different temperatures.
A student says the plant should run at 350 °C because the yield is highest.
Evaluate this suggestion.
markScheme: 1 mark: the yield at 350 °C is higher (52% compared with 28%)
1 mark: but the rate would be much slower, so less ammonia would be produced per hour; 450 °C is a better compromise
questions.explanation: Industry cares about the amount of ammonia made per unit time, not just the equilibrium yield.

questions.question: In which state is ammonia removed from the Haber process?
markScheme: 1 mark: Liquid
questions.explanation: Cooling liquefies the ammonia so it can be removed; nitrogen and hydrogen remain as gases.

questions.question: State the temperature used in the Haber process.
markScheme: 1 mark: about 450 °C
questions.explanation: About 450 °C is a compromise temperature.
